passage: Listen, beta, Ganga Nani is going to tell you something. When I was fourteen, my friend Damini joined the swimming class at the canal-side club. The first month was all fun. Then the coach began teaching the breathing turn, and Damini swallowed water twice and coughed for ten minutes. She stopped coming. "It is boring," she said, "just lap after lap." I noticed she never once said it was hard. The coach came to her house and offered to move her to the shallow group for two weeks. She said no. The next summer I swam across the canal with the others, and Damini stood on the bank holding towels. Years later she told me, "I left right before it got good."

qa.q: What did Damini say when she stopped coming to swimming class?
qa.a: Damini said, "It is boring, just lap after lap."

qa.q: What was Damini probably feeling when she swallowed water and then called class boring?
qa.a: Discouraged and uncomfortable, but she called it boredom and never said it was hard.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Damini have chosen differently?
qa.a: When the coach offered the shallow group for two weeks; accepting would have let her stay through the hard part.

qa.q: How might the coach have felt when Damini said no?
qa.a: Disappointed and concerned, having come to her house and offered a gentler way to keep going.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who leaves a class as soon as it becomes hard, calls it boredom and later regrets leaving before it got good.

passage: Rain hammered the tin roof of the school shed, and the district trial was two days away. Damini had missed three penalty saves in a row since the coach moved her to goalkeeper, and her gloves were soaked. "This is boring," she announced, dropping them by the bench. "I want to go home." Rukmini, holding the umbrella over both girls, stared at her. "You were not bored on Monday when you played striker." Damini shrugged and walked off toward the bus stop, where the bus was already late and packed. She counted her coins for the fare and thought about what she had said. On Thursday she did not turn up for the trial, and the team drew lots for a substitute keeper.

qa.q: How many penalty saves in a row had Damini missed?
qa.a: Damini had missed three penalty saves in a row.

qa.q: What was Damini really feeling when she called practice boring?
qa.a: Frustrated and discouraged by the missed saves, which she labelled as boredom.

qa.q: What could Damini try before deciding to leave?
qa.a: Ask the coach for extra keeper practice or a short break, and still go to the trial.

qa.q: How might Rukmini feel as Damini walks off?
qa.a: Puzzled and worried, since Rukmini points out that Damini was not bored on Monday.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who drops a sport position at the first real difficulty and calls it boredom.

passage:
"I'm quitting guitar," Farhan announced, dropping his case by the door.
His sister Shreya looked up from her laptop. "Since when?"
"Since today. It's boring."
"Last week you played me three songs and said it was the best thing ever."
"That was before barre chords."
"What are barre chords?"
"You have to press all six strings with one finger. It hurts. It sounds terrible. I've been trying for two weeks."
"So it's not boring. It's hard."
Farhan scowled. "Same thing."
"Not really. Remember when I wanted to quit swimming at the deep end?"
"You cried."
"I cried. And then I could swim." Shreya closed the laptop. "Some things are right to quit. But if you quit exactly where it gets hard, you never find out what's on the other side."
Farhan looked at his case. "Maybe I'll try one more month."
"One month. Then decide."

qa.q: How long had Farhan been trying barre chords?
qa.a: I've been trying for two weeks.

qa.q: How does Farhan really feel about guitar right now?
qa.a: Farhan feels frustrated and discouraged by the painful barre chords, though he calls it boredom.

qa.q: What does Shreya suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Shreya suggests one more month before deciding, because quitting right at the hard part would stop Farhan's growth just before he gets past it.

qa.q: How does Shreya use her own story to help?
qa.a: Shreya shares that she cried at the deep end but kept going and learned to swim, showing that discomfort can come just before progress.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who wants to quit guitar the moment it gets hard, calling it boredom, and a sister who helps him see the difference.

passage:
I quit swimming three times before I was fifteen. I'm Kalyani, and I always said the same thing: "It's boring."
It wasn't boring. What happened each time was the same. I'd enjoy the first weeks, splashing and floating. Then the coach, Madhav sir, would start on breathing: face in the water, turn, breathe, face in. I'd swallow water. I'd feel stupid next to the kids who could already do it. And I'd stop going.
The third time, Madhav sir called my mother. He said, "She's not bored. She's stuck at the hard part. Everybody is."
My mother made me a deal: stay until I could do one full length with breathing, then decide.
It took seven weeks. I swallowed a lot of pool water. Then one Tuesday, I did the length. I held the wall at the end, gasping and grinning.
I still swim. I'm not a champion. But I know now that "boring" was sometimes my word for "hard."

qa.q: How long did it take Kalyani to do one full length with breathing?
qa.a: It took seven weeks.

qa.q: How did Kalyani feel when the breathing lessons started?
qa.a: Kalyani felt stupid and discouraged next to kids who could already do it.

qa.q: What deal helped Kalyani get past the hard part?
qa.a: Staying until she could do one full length with breathing, then deciding, which gave her a clear point to reach before quitting.

qa.q: How did Madhav sir see Kalyani's quitting?
qa.a: Madhav sir saw that she was stuck at the hard part, not bored, and cared enough to call her mother.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who repeatedly quit swimming at the first difficulty, calling it boredom, until a deal helped her push through.

passage:
Football coach's note, under-16 squad, October.
Francis joined in June. He was quick and loved the matches. In September we began fitness sessions: sprints, shuttles, core work. After the second week, he told me, "This is boring, coach. I just want to play."
He missed the next three sessions. His friend Lalit told me Francis was thinking of quitting.
I've seen this often. The fitness block is where many boys drop out, just before it starts to pay off. I did not want to lecture him, so I asked him to watch one match from the bench. In the second half, our two fittest players ran past a tired defence twice.
After the match Francis came to me. "If I do the sprints, will I get that fast?"
"Faster than now," I said. "But only if you stay past the hard part."
He came back on Monday. He's still complaining. He's also still coming.
— Coach, Under-16

qa.q: When did the fitness sessions begin?
qa.a: In September.

qa.q: How did Francis feel about the fitness sessions?
qa.a: Francis felt bored and frustrated, just wanting to play matches instead.

qa.q: Why was showing Francis the match wiser than a lecture?
qa.a: It let Francis see for himself what fitness could do, so staying past the hard part felt worth it.

qa.q: How might Lalit have felt telling the coach about Francis?
qa.a: Lalit was probably worried about losing a friend from the team and hoped the coach could help.

grounding: Shows a teenager who wants to quit football when training gets hard, calling it boredom, and a coach who helps him stay.

passage:
Saturday.
Told Naveen Sir today I'm not coming to swimming anymore. Said it's boring. Same lanes, same whistle, same chlorine smell.
It wasn't boring in the first month. I loved the kicking drills, and I was faster than the two others from my class. Then this week he started us on butterfly stroke. I swallowed half the pool. The little kids in the next lane laughed. My shoulders ached all evening.
Naveen Sir said, "Everyone looks like a drowning cat for the first three weeks. Give it till the end of the month." I said I've got too much homework.
It's the same as keyboard last year. I stopped when we reached chords with both hands. And badminton, when the smashes started.
Maybe I'm just someone who gets bored. Or maybe I leave right when it gets hard. I don't really want to think about which.
Hafsa

qa.q: Which stroke did Naveen Sir start this week?
qa.a: Butterfly stroke.

qa.q: What was Hafsa really feeling when calling swimming boring?
qa.a: Hafsa seems embarrassed and discouraged after swallowing water, aching shoulders and being laughed at, and "boring" covers that discomfort.

qa.q: What could Hafsa try before deciding to stop?
qa.a: Hafsa could take Naveen Sir's offer, stay till the end of the month, and decide once the first hard weeks are over.

qa.q: How might Naveen Sir see Hafsa leaving now?
qa.a: He likely sees a swimmer quitting just before the stroke gets easier, which is why he says everyone looks like a drowning cat for the first three weeks.

grounding: Shows a teenager dropping an activity as soon as it gets difficult and calling it boredom, a pattern repeated before.
